extracted.intended_audience: state and local policymakers, program administrators, and practitioners designing or funding responsible fatherhood / non-custodial parent employment and support programs
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for designing, funding, and operating programs that connect low-income non-custodial fathers to employment, legal help, parenting education, and supportive services; includes policy recommendations for governors, legislators, and state agencies about use of TANF, WtW, WIA and other funding.

rubrics_metrics.name: Require employment programs to partner with parenting programs
rubrics_metrics.description: State workforce development and welfare agencies should require employment programs receiving state funds to partner with or provide referrals to parenting programs for non-custodial fathers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Conversely, state health and welfare agencies should require parenting education programs to link their activities with programs that focus on employment and training.

rubrics_metrics.name: Court referral of men with child-support arrearages
rubrics_metrics.description: Governors and legislators should require state and county courts to refer men with child-support arrearages to employment programs, as the federal welfare reform law gives states authority to do.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use court referrals to connect fathers under enforcement to employment and training services rather than only punitive responses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Child support enforcement coordination and modification orders
rubrics_metrics.description: Governors and legislators should require child support enforcement offices to coordinate with responsible fatherhood programs and pursue modification orders for low-income fathers who are making good-faith efforts to find and keep jobs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Coordinate enforcement offices with program providers to adjust orders for fathers participating in employment programs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use TANF to fund legal assistance partnerships
rubrics_metrics.description: Governors and legislators should use TANF funds to provide grants that enable employment and training programs for low-income men and women to hire lawyers or develop partnerships with legal services offices that help clients overcome legal barriers to employment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Legal help can negotiate fines/penalties, seal/expunge records, fight evictions, and facilitate bankruptcy—barriers that impede employment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Maintain active employer relationships and vacancy tracking
rubrics_metrics.description: Program staff should develop relationships with area employers and agencies, keep track of each agency’s vacancies and eligibility requirements, and refer fathers directly to employers with jobs available.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Marion County program cultivated relationships with 29 employers and referred participants directly; staff track vacancies and eligibility and match clients accordingly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Refer participants with barriers to training or community service
rubrics_metrics.description: Refer men with barriers to employment such as criminal records or low skills to job training programs or community service with the city.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Programs should triage clients—direct-job placements for those ready, training or service for those with deficits or records.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide mediation and flexible support orders for young fathers
rubrics_metrics.description: Programs should run mediation and help fathers under age 25 obtain flexible support orders so that they can stay in school.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Flexible support orders can facilitate education completion and longer-term employability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comprehensive employment services (resume, interview, training, placement, retention)
rubrics_metrics.description: Programs should provide resumé and interview preparation, job-search assistance, short-term training, on-the-job training, and job retention services.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The FATHER Project and others combine these services with placement and follow-up; retention services (follow-up, hotlines) are essential.

rubrics_metrics.name: Intensive one-on-one case management ('father advocates')
rubrics_metrics.description: Use father advocates to work one-on-one with fathers, providing intensive case management services and individualized support (rides, references, help to attend interviews).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Intensive advocacy helps overcome small practical barriers and provides continuity for hard-to-serve fathers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Offer legal seminars and sliding-fee referral networks
rubrics_metrics.description: Sponsor regular legal seminars (low fee or waived for hardship) and refer parents who need representation to a network of lawyers who charge sliding fees or hourly rates.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide accessible legal advice on paternity, child support, visitation rights, and referral pathways to affordable counsel.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use a mix of incentives and sanctions to encourage participation
rubrics_metrics.description: Programs can use both carrots and sticks: recruit volunteers and court-ordered participants, and for those who refuse, seek sanctions (e.g., jail); for those who participate, offer incentives (e.g., lowered support obligations).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Santa Clara example: lowered monthly child support to $50 for participants; refusal could lead to jail—combination motivates engagement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide job-retention supports such as 24-hour hotlines
rubrics_metrics.description: Provide employment and counseling services with extra features such as a 24-hour job retention hotline to help fathers keep jobs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Retention supports after placement (hotlines, follow-up services) increase sustained employment.

rubrics_metrics.name: STRIVE-style intensive job-preparation (boot camp)
rubrics_metrics.description: Implement intensive job-preparation courses modeled on STRIVE: multi-week, full-day 'attitude training' focusing on professional dress, interview performance, respectful communication, and taking direction from supervisors, followed by placement and multi-year retention services.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: STRIVE example: three-week, eight-hours-a-day program with two years of retention services and placement assistance; applicable to both men and women.

rubrics_metrics.name: Peer support groups with nonjudgmental facilitation
rubrics_metrics.description: Facilitate peer groups that discuss manhood and fatherhood, led by a facilitator who asks probing questions, prods participation, and refrains from judgment—starting from the positive assumption that participants want to be good fathers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Peer groups build social support, model positive behavior, and connect discussion to practical skill-building and employment goals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interagency cooperation and case conferencing
rubrics_metrics.description: Programs should establish interagency cooperation (D.A., welfare department, employment agencies) and regular case conferencing where staff share information to develop client plans and discuss progress.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Los Angeles PFS success attributed to close cooperation and shared client information across agencies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use incentive structures (lowering obligations, reinstating licenses)
rubrics_metrics.description: Offer concrete incentives for program completion—e.g., lower child-support obligations to $50/month and reinstate suspended driver's licenses for participants who stick with the program.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tangible incentives increase voluntary participation and program retention.

rubrics_metrics.name: Address criminal-record barriers through honesty and employer partnerships
rubrics_metrics.description: Advise clients to be honest with employers about criminal records and cultivate employer relationships willing to give participants second chances.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Programs should coach clients on disclosure and stigma management and build employer networks receptive to hiring ex-offenders.

rubrics_metrics.name: TANF/MOE funds as primary flexible funding source
rubrics_metrics.description: The TANF block grant is the single best funding source for fatherhood programs; states may use federal block grant and MOE funds for any activity that accomplishes the broad purposes of welfare reform (ending dependence, promoting employment, encouraging two-parent families, reducing out-of-wedlock pregnancies).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: States have latitude to define 'needy' differently for different services; services not meeting 'basic needs' are not subject to federal time limits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Permissible uses of TANF and SSBG funds for fathers
rubrics_metrics.description: States may use TANF and SSBG funds to provide employment assistance, job training, substance abuse treatment, mentoring, counseling, marriage counseling, mediation, transportation, child care, access and visitation services, and child support pass-throughs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: List of allowable services provides program designers a menu for funding components essential to serving non-custodial fathers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Welfare-to-Work block grant eligibility criteria and permitted services
rubrics_metrics.description: States may spend WtW funds on employment services for any non-custodial parents who (1) are unemployed/underemployed/having difficulty paying child support, (2) have minor children who received TANF in the past year or are eligible for food stamps/SSI/Medicaid/CHIP, and (3) sign personal responsibility contracts committing to paternity, support, and participation in employment services.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Permitted uses include job readiness classes, on-the-job training, up to six months of vocational training, subsidized work, and job-retention services.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use Workforce Investment Act and DOL demonstration authority
rubrics_metrics.description: State workforce development agencies should apply to the U.S. Department of Labor to launch non-custodial fathers demonstration projects under the Workforce Investment Act and use DOL demonstration authority to develop specialized methods for serving fathers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: WIA's one-stop system may leave fathers behind; demonstrations can pilot specialized approaches without fear of penalties.

rubrics_metrics.name: Set aside TANF/WtW percentages and reserve bonuses for fathers
rubrics_metrics.description: Governors and legislators should set aside a percentage of TANF and Welfare-to-Work funds for programs that serve low-income non-custodial parents and should reserve any bonuses the state receives under TANF or Title IV-D to serve non-custodial parents.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explicitly earmarking funds ensures sustained investment in fatherhood programs amid competing priorities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Simplify and broaden eligibility rules for non-custodial parents
rubrics_metrics.description: Governors and legislators should revise and simplify eligibility requirements for non-custodial parents to participate in TANF-funded programs—for example, make mediation, custody/visitation services, and parenting classes available to any parent regardless of income; make employment services available to unemployed/underemployed parents whose child qualifies for CHIP.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: States can and should adopt more inclusive eligibility definitions to reach fathers who fall outside narrow welfare categories.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ensure parity of services for non-custodial parents under state programs
rubrics_metrics.description: Use state WtW and WIA funds to ensure non-custodial parents with children on TANF receive the same help getting and keeping jobs that custodial parents on TANF get (eligibility for any non-custodial parent with a child on TANF).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Coordinate child support enforcement offices and welfare agencies to identify and refer eligible fathers to local training and placement services.

rubrics_metrics.name: Forgive or decrease TANF-related child support debt for participating fathers
rubrics_metrics.description: Governors and legislators should forgive or decrease TANF-related child support debt for fathers who participate in programs designed to increase their earnings and improve their parenting skills.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Debt forgiveness (or suspension/reduction) for state-owed arrears can create incentives and realistic opportunities for fathers to restart regular payments to families.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dedicate child support revenues to fund fatherhood programs
rubrics_metrics.description: Governors and legislators should dedicate revenues from TANF-related child support collections to fund responsible fatherhood programs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Using a portion of collections can sustain programs and align enforcement dollars with service investments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rewrite child support guidelines to allow self-support reserves
rubrics_metrics.description: Governors and legislators should rewrite state child support guidelines to allow self-support reserves for non-custodial working parents.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Self-support reserves permit non-custodial parents to retain a portion of income to live on, protecting low-income working fathers from overwhelming obligations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Amend state EITC to credit non-custodial parents who pay support
rubrics_metrics.description: Governors and legislators should amend their state Earned Income Tax Credits to give fathers credit for the child support they pay (options include allowing non-custodial parents who meet support obligations to claim the EITC, giving custodial priority but enabling fathers to claim when custodial parent is ineligible, or giving fathers half the credit or up to the amount of support paid).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Three policy options are suggested to create tax-based incentives for fathers to work and pay support; credit designs should cap at amount of support paid and require full payment to qualify.

rubrics_metrics.name: Include clear contact information in enforcement notices
rubrics_metrics.description: In every notice mailed out, child support enforcement offices should include a telephone number fathers can call if they want to contest paternity, seek modification of a child support order, or negotiate custody and visitation issues.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide an accessible point of contact to reduce procedural barriers and enable fathers to engage with the system constructively.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reinstate or strengthen child support pass-throughs
rubrics_metrics.description: States should reinstate their state's child support pass-throughs or strengthen existing pass-throughs to allow at least some of the child support paid by low-income fathers to be paid directly to their families.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pass-throughs increase incentives for fathers to cooperate with support systems and ensure payments benefit children rather than exclusively repaying state TANF costs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Suspend, reduce, or forgive state-owed child support debt for program participants
rubrics_metrics.description: States have discretion to suspend, reduce, or forgive any child support debts that are owed to the state (not the family); TANF-related child support debts could be waived for fathers who participate in employment and fatherhood programs and subsequently maintain up-to-date payments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Washington forgives state debt for reunification with hardship; Vermont suspends payments when combined incomes are below threshold—policies aimed at giving fathers a chance to start anew.
